t.1.155.1: King Drupada, unforgiving and resentful, wandered among many dwellings of brahmins, seeking bulls among the twice-born who were accomplished in sacred rites.
t.1.155.2: Longing for the birth of a son, his mind stricken with grief, he constantly brooded: "I have no excellent offspring."
t.1.155.3: Out of despair he said to the sons that had been born to him, “Shame on such kinsmen!” and, longing to retaliate against Droṇa, he was given over to heavy sighing.
t.1.155.4: Reflecting on Droṇa's might, his discipline, his training and his deeds, the best of kings, though he strove, could find no way to retaliate against him by warrior strength, O Bhārata.
t.1.155.5: Then that lord of the earth, wandering about near the Kalmāṣī on the bank of the Gaṅgā, came upon a holy dwelling of brāhmaṇas.
t.1.155.6: There was no twice-born there who was not a snātaka, none without vows, and likewise none who was not greatly blessed; and there he saw two men of rigorous vows.
t.1.155.7: The son of Pṛṣata found the two brahmarṣis Yāja and Upayāja, men of tranquil mind, devoted to the study of the Saṃhitā, and both Kāśyapas by lineage.
t.1.155.8: Those two brāhmaṇas, the best of seers, were well suited to bring about his deliverance; and he, unwearied, entreated them, offering every object of desire.
t.1.155.9: Having discerned the strength and wisdom of the two, he approached the younger, Upayāja, firm in his vows, in private, tempting him with all that he might desire.
t.1.155.10: Devoted to serving his feet, speaking pleasantly and granting every desire, he honored Upayāja in the proper manner and then spoke to him.
t.1.155.11: O Brahmin Upayāja, when that rite has been performed by which a son may be born to me for the death of Droṇa, I shall give you a hundred million cows.
t.1.155.12: Or whatever else, O best of the twice-born, would be very dear to your heart, all that I will give to you; of this I have no doubt.
t.1.155.13: Thus addressed, the seer replied to him, "Not I." Then Drupada, intending to win his favor, attended upon him once again.
t.1.155.14: Then, at the end of a year, O king, that best of the twice-born, Upayāja, spoke at the proper time to Drupada in a sweet voice.
t.1.155.15: My elder brother, while wandering by a forest stream, picked up a fruit that had fallen on ground whose purity was unknown.
t.1.155.16: While following my brother, I saw that unseemly conduct of his: he would by no means show any scruple in taking up what is impure.
t.1.155.17: Having seen the fruit, he did not see the faults bound up with it. How could one who does not discern purity in this matter be any different elsewhere?
t.1.155.18: He who, while studying the Saṃhitā and dwelling in his teacher's house, constantly eats alms-food that is the leavings of others, praising again and again the virtue of the food, and without any disgust.
t.1.155.20: Feeling disgust and pondering this in his mind, the king, knower of all dharma, having heard the words of Upayāja, duly honored the seer Yāja, who was worthy of honor, and spoke to him.
t.1.155.19: Judging by the eye of reasoning, I consider that brother of mine to be one who seeks reward. Go to him, O king; he will perform the sacrifice for you.
t.1.155.21: I will give you eighty thousand cows; perform the sacrifice for me, O lord! You ought to bring relief to me, who am tormented by enmity with Droṇa.
t.1.155.22: For he is the best of the knowers of brahman and unsurpassed in the brahmāstra as well; that is why Droṇa defeated me in that quarrel between friends.
t.1.155.23: There is no kṣatriya on earth, however foremost, who is equal to him, the wise Bhāradvāja, chief among the teachers of the Kauravas.
t.1.155.24: Droṇa's nets of arrows, which carry off the bodies of living beings, and his bow, six cubits long, great and unequalled, are seen.
t.1.155.25: For that great archer, the high-minded Bhāradvāja, without doubt repels the force of a kṣatriya with the force of a brahmin.
t.1.155.26: Ordained for the destruction of the kṣatriyas, he stands firm like Jāmadagnya; for the power of his weapons is terrible, not to be withstood by men on earth.
t.1.155.27: Raising his brahmanical splendor like a fire fed with oblations, he, with the brahman power at his forefront, meets the kṣatra in battle and burns it up. When brahman and kṣatra are set against each other, it is the splendor of the brahman that excels.
t.1.155.28: Lacking in kṣatriya strength, I have sought refuge in the power of a brahmin, having come to you, who surpass Droṇa and are the foremost among the knowers of brahman.
t.1.155.29: May I obtain a son who will be the slayer of Droṇa, invincible in battle. Perform that rite for me, Yāja, and I will give you a hundred million cows.
t.1.155.31: Then Upayāja, of great austerity, explained to that lord of men a sacrificial rite performed with the sacred fires, for the fruit of a son.
t.1.155.30: Saying “So be it” to him, Yāja set about arranging the purpose of his patron, and he urged the unwilling Upayāja, saying, “It is for the sake of your elder.” And so Yāja pledged himself to the destruction of Droṇa.
t.1.155.32: And that son, of great valour, great splendour and great strength, will be for you, O king, just such a one as is desired.
t.1.155.33: Intent upon a slayer of Bhāradvāja, King Drupada gathered all those things accordingly for the success of the rite.
t.1.155.34: At the end of the oblation Yāja then summoned the queen: "Come to me, O queen Pṛṣatī! A pair of children has come to you."
t.1.155.35: My face is anointed, O brahmin, and I am wearing sacred perfumes; I am held back by the purpose of obtaining a son. Wait, Yāja, for my sake.
t.1.155.37: When Yāja had spoken thus and the consecrated oblation had been offered, there rose up from that fire a boy resembling a god.
t.1.155.36: The oblation has been cooked by Yāja and consecrated with mantras by Upayāja; how could it fail to fulfill the desire? So you may come forward or stay where you are.
t.1.155.38: Flame-colored and terrible in form, wearing a diadem and bearing excellent armor, armed with sword and arrows, holding a bow, he roared again and again.
t.1.155.39: He mounted the excellent chariot and then set out in it. Thereupon the Pāñcālas, overjoyed, shouted aloud, "Well done, well done!"
t.1.155.40: "This prince, dispeller of fear, bringer of glory to the Pāñcālas, remover of the king's grief, has been born for the slaying of Droṇa," so spoke then a great invisible being moving in the sky.
t.1.155.41: And a maiden too, Pāñcālī, rose up from the middle of the altar: fortunate, lovely of limb, with a waist slender as an altar, and enchanting to the mind.
t.1.155.43: She whose fragrance, like that of the blue lotus, wafts forth for a krośa, who bears a supreme beauty, and for whom there is no equal on earth.
t.1.155.42: Dark-complexioned, with eyes like lotus petals and dark curling hair, she had taken on a human form, yet she plainly bore the beauty of an immortal.
t.1.155.44: And when that fair-hipped maiden was born, a bodiless voice spoke concerning her: "This Kṛṣṇā, the best of all women, will lead the kṣatriyas to destruction."
t.1.155.45: In time this slender-waisted woman will accomplish the work of the gods; because of her, a great terror will arise for the kṣatriyas.
t.1.155.46: Hearing that, all the Pāñcālas roared like a pride of lions, and this earth could not bear them, so filled with joy were they.
t.1.155.47: Seeing the two, Pṛṣatī, longing for children, approached Yāja, saying, "May these two never know any mother other than me."
t.1.155.49: "Because of his boldness, his exceeding daring, and his birth from fire together with the splendour of righteousness, let this prince of Drupada be called Dhṛṣṭadyumna."
t.1.155.48: "So be it," Yāja said to her, wishing to do what would please the king. And the twice-born, their hearts fully content, gave names to the two of them.
t.1.155.50: They called her Kṛṣṇā, for she was dark in complexion. Thus was that twin pair born at the great sacrifice of Drupada.
t.1.155.52: For the great-minded Droṇa, deeming that destiny which is bound to come cannot be escaped, acted thus out of concern to protect his own fame.
t.1.155.51: But the mighty Bhāradvāja brought Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the Pāñcāla prince, to his own dwelling and took him on as a pupil for the sake of instruction in weapons.
